posts.title: Twenty-two walks, twenty-two guides
posts.hook: The launch post. Lead with the idea, not the technology.
posts.linkedin:
We built something we wanted to exist.

Twenty-two walking tours through cities that are gone. London in the week of the Great Fire. Rome in the Jubilee of 1600. Stockholm when the harbour ran on copper. Colombo when cinnamon paid for everything. Istanbul in the year a fire took half of it.

Each one is led by somebody who actually lived there. Not a narrator. A flower seller on Ludgate Hill who buys violets before six. A waterman who rowed families away from the fire. A midwife who is let into every house in her quarter. A seamstress who watched the wall come down at Porta Pia and kept her opinions to herself, because half her customers were on one side and half on the other.

You can interrupt them and ask questions. They answer in their own voice, and they know nothing about the world after their own year.

Twenty-two are live now, across seven cities. Where should we go next?
posts.instagram:
Twenty-two walks through cities that no longer exist, and twenty-two people who lived in them.

London 1666. Rome 1600. Stockholm 1650. Colombo 1700. Istanbul 1660.

Each walk is led by someone who was there. You can stop them and ask.

Where should we go next? 👇

posts.title: Film: Walk back in time
posts.hook: Fifteen seconds of the experience itself, built from the walk's own scenes and Caterina's own voice. Post with sound on.
posts.linkedin:
Turn your sound on for this one.

This is fifteen seconds of Rome in the year 1600. The market you can hear is Campo de' Fiori. The voice is Caterina Ruspoli, the herb seller who leads the walk, and everything on screen is our own reconstruction of her city.

There is no film crew behind this, and no stock footage in it. It is the actual fabric of the tour: the scenes you walk through, the woman who talks to you, the street noise around her. We just let it speak for itself for fifteen seconds.

The product is this feeling, held across five or six stops, with a guide you can interrupt and question at any moment.

Twenty-two walks. London, Rome, Stockholm, Colombo, Istanbul, Gothenburg and Paris. app.worldasitwas.com

posts.title: The portraits move
posts.hook: The craft post. People stop for a face that looks back.
posts.linkedin:
A portrait that holds still reads as a photograph. A portrait that looks up and finds you reads as a person.

So our guides do the second thing. Their attention wanders while they talk: they glance off at something in their own street, come back to you, smile, get on with their work. Forty seconds of it, so it never comes round often enough to notice.

The engineering detail we got wrong first is a good one. To make a clip loop seamlessly, the obvious instruction is that it must end in the pose it started in. That instruction is why our first attempt barely moved: told to end exactly where she began, the model does as little as possible in between.

We removed the constraint and closed the loop afterwards in code instead, by dissolving the end back into the start. Measured movement went up by a factor of thirty.

The lesson generalises: if your output looks lifeless, check whether you asked for it.
posts.instagram:
She looks up. She finds you. She smiles and goes back to her herbs.

Forty seconds, looping, so you never catch it repeating.

Rome, 1600. 🕯️

posts.title: You can interrupt them
posts.hook: The differentiator. This is the thing no audio guide does.
posts.linkedin:
Every audio guide has the same problem. It talks, you listen, and if you have a question you keep it.

Ours can be interrupted. Hold the button and ask, and the person you are walking with answers you in her own voice, out of her own life. Ask Caterina what a friar being burned in her square smelled like and she will tell you, because she was there in February and she sells herbs twenty feet from where it happened.

What she will not do is tell you anything about the world after 1600. She has never heard of a photograph. She does not know the Jubilee ends.

That boundary is the whole design. A guide who knows everything is a search engine with a voice. A guide who knows only what she could know is a person.

🎙️

posts.title: Everything is sourced
posts.hook: The trust post. Aimed at museums, educators, partners.
posts.linkedin:
The fastest way to make historical content is to let a model improvise. We do the opposite, and it costs us.

Every stop on every walk is researched first, against archives and primary sources, and the reconstructions are built from that research. When Nell tells you what a bunch of violets cost outside St Paul's in 1850, that price came from somewhere, and the walk will show you where.

It is slower. It is more expensive. It is the only version worth building, because the moment one detail is invented, the listener is right to doubt all of them.

If you work in a museum or an archive and this is interesting to you, I would like to talk.
posts.instagram:
Every price, every street, every date: sourced.

It would be faster to make it up. It would also be worthless. 📚
posts.twitter:
The fast way to make historical content is to let the model improvise.

We research every stop against archives first, then build from that.

Slower and dearer. But the moment one detail is invented, the listener is right to doubt all of them.

posts.title: The same building, forty-four years apart
posts.hook: Two walks, two guides, one unfinished mosque. Neither of them sees it done.
posts.linkedin:
On the left is Eminönü in 1616. On the right is the same shore in 1660.

The building is the same building. It was begun in 1597 for a Valide Sultan and the work stopped when the power behind it did. Yusuf, the water carrier who leads our 1616 walk, passes the stalled shell every day on his way down to the boats, and calls it the mosque that was left stranded when her son died and they shut her away.

Forty-four years later Emine, the midwife who leads our 1660 walk, stands on the same shore after the fire that took a great part of the city, and the work has started again. The Valide is paying, and a market of stone is going up beside it so the rents can feed the mosque afterwards. Emine is glad of the wages and clear-eyed about the rest: if your house burned, this work may give you wages, but it will not give you your old lane back.

Neither of them ever sees it finished. It opens in 1665.

We did not plan this. The two walks were built separately, one about water and one about a fire, and the building was simply standing there in both, at the stage it had actually reached. That is what you get when you reconstruct a city rather than a story. It keeps its own continuity, and the people walking through it do not know what happens next.

Both walks are live. Istanbul is our fifth city.
posts.instagram:
Left: 1616. Right: 1660. The same building.

Begun in 1597, abandoned when the money behind it died. Our water carrier passes the shell every day. Forty-four years later our midwife watches it rise again out of the ash of a fire.

Neither of them lives to see it open. That happens in 1665. 🕌

Istanbul, twice.

posts.title: One city, three centuries
posts.hook: Colombo in 1700, 1905 and 1999, and the same job done three ways.
posts.linkedin:
Three walks through Colombo, and the thing that ties two of them together is not a building. It is a job.

In 1700 Kumari works the cinnamon coast, where the peeling of bark pays for a colony. In 1905 Sena pulls a rickshaw through the Fort, ten hours a day barefoot on hot tar, renting the vehicle by the day from a man who owns thirty of them. In 1999 Ranjith drives a red Bajaj three-wheeler through the same Fort, renting it by the day from a man in Dematagoda, paying the owner and the petrol before he earns a rupee for himself.

Ninety-four years separate Sena and Ranjith, and the trade is identical: carry somebody through the city for a fare, on a vehicle you do not own.

The city is not identical at all. Sena's Fort is a coaling station of the empire and everything in it is arriving or leaving. Ranjith's Fort is sealed behind barriers and sandbags after a bomb, and he can only nose in to the edge and let the passenger walk the last part.

This is why we build a city more than once. One walk shows you what a place looked like. Three of them show you what changed, and the far more interesting thing, which is what did not.

Colombo 1700, 1905 and 1999. All three are live.
posts.instagram:
1700, 1905, 1999. One city.

The rickshaw man and the three-wheeler driver are ninety-four years apart and doing the same job: carry somebody across town, on a vehicle you rent by the day.

The job did not change. The Fort did. 🛺

Colombo.
posts.twitter:

The trade didn't change. The city did.

posts.title: The same lane, four hundred years apart
posts.hook: Every stop carries the spot as it stands today, and the now picture is never allowed to be a reconstruction.
posts.linkedin:
Left: a lane on the third hill in Istanbul, climbing towards the Süleymaniye, in 1616. It is from our walk with Yusuf, the water carrier, and the street fountain in the foreground is where he fills up.

Right: a photograph of the same lane.

Every stop on every walk carries this pair, and it is the most useful thing a reconstruction can do, because it tells you where you are. On its own a historical picture is a nice painting. Beside the photograph it becomes somewhere you could walk this afternoon, and four hundred years stops being a number you were told and becomes a distance you can feel.

It is also the honest move, and we made it a rule rather than a habit. The schema the walks are built against will not publish a then-and-now card whose now picture is a reconstruction. It has to be a photograph or an archive item, credited, with its licence recorded. That one on the right is Arild Vågen's, from Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

So the deal we are offering is visible in the picture itself: here is our version of a year nobody photographed, and here, immediately beside it, is the evidence you can go and check.

Twenty-two walks across seven cities.
posts.instagram:
Left: a lane below the Süleymaniye in 1616, with the fountain our water carrier fills at.
Right: a photograph of the same lane.

Every stop carries this pair. The right-hand half is never a reconstruction, by rule: it has to be a real credited photograph, or the walk will not publish. 🕌

Istanbul.

posts.title: The hard part is what must not be in the picture
posts.hook: The craft post. Reconstruction is mostly subtraction, and the missing thing is what a local spots first.
posts.linkedin:
This is Galle Road in Colombo in 1999, from the walk we published this week. The thing worth noticing is what is not in it.

There are no glass towers on this road. Not one. Today that same stretch has them, and so does almost every photograph of Colombo you can find, which means a reconstruction left to itself will put them in. So the brief for this scene spends more words forbidding than describing: two and three storey shophouses with shutters and signboards, the odd plain 1970s block of flats, the coastal railway on the sea side behind a low wall, no high rise anywhere, and if any tall building shows at all it is the Fort skyline far to the north, small and hazy.

We write that kind of instruction constantly. The Golden Horn in 1616 has no bridge across it. The great mosque at Eminönü in 1660 is not a mosque yet, it is bare stone and scaffolding and lime pits. The burnt quarter has no flames in it, because the fire is over and the ash is cold.

Research tells you what was there. Something close to half the work is naming what was not there yet, because the anachronism is the first thing a person who knows the city will catch, and once they catch one they are right to doubt all the rest.

Twenty-two walks, seven cities.
posts.instagram:
Galle Road, Colombo, 1999. Look at what is not there.

No glass towers. Anywhere. Today that road has them, so a reconstruction will happily add them unless you forbid it, in writing, every single time.

The Golden Horn in 1616 has no bridge. The mosque in 1660 is not finished. The fire is out.

Research tells you what was there. Half the job is naming what was not. 🚌
posts.twitter:
Galle Road, Colombo, 1999. The point is what's missing: no glass towers, anywhere.

That road has them today, so a reconstruction adds them unless you forbid it in writing.

Research tells you what was there. Half the work is naming what wasn't.

posts.title: Nobody in these walks is important
posts.hook: Why every guide is somebody carrying something, and never a king.
posts.linkedin:
We have twenty-two guides now and not one of them is important.

A water carrier filling a leather skin at a fountain. A three-wheeler driver with his hand on the bar and the meter beside it. A herb seller. A porter on a quay stacked with copper. Rickshaw men waiting outside a hotel. A midwife at a door that is not hers.

No kings, no generals, no architects. It is a rule, not an accident, and there are two reasons for it.

The first is access. The people who see the most of a city are the ones who move through all of it and get let in everywhere. A midwife is admitted to Muslim, Greek, Armenian and Jewish houses alike, because a birth does not wait for anyone to agree about religion. A water carrier climbs into courtyards belonging to people who would never invite him to dinner. A driver hears what gets said in the back seat once the passenger has forgotten he is there.

The second is that important people come with a script. Ask a general about a battle and you get the version that survived. Ask the man who carries the water what the battle did to his round, and you get the day.

Six of them at work, above. All twenty-two walks are live.
posts.instagram:
Twenty-two guides and not one of them is important.

A water carrier. A three-wheeler driver. A herb seller. A porter. A rickshaw man. A midwife.

The people who see the most of a city are the ones who move through all of it and get let in everywhere. 🪣

Seven cities.
posts.twitter:
Twenty-two guides and not one is important: a water carrier, a driver, a herb seller, a porter, a midwife.

The people who see most of a city are the ones let in everywhere.

Ask a general about a battle, you get the surviving version. Ask the water carrier, you get the day.

posts.title: He does not know how any of it ends
posts.hook: The strongest thing in the Colombo walk is a question the guide cannot answer, and you can.
posts.linkedin:
That banner says MILLENNIUM PARTY, 1999 to 2000. It is hanging at Town Hall in Colombo in the last weeks of December, days after a bomb at an election rally, and Ranjith is driving past it with a fare in the back who wants to talk about whether the computers will stop at midnight.

He does not know. He cannot know. Ask him and he will tell you what people in his back seat are saying, which is roughly what people everywhere were saying, and then he will get on with the junction.

We have written before about why our guides know nothing after their own year. That is a design rule, and its job is to stop a guide becoming a search engine with a voice. What we did not expect was how it feels from the other side of it.

You know. He does not. You know the computers are fine. You know how long the war has left to run. He is worried about the first, has no idea about the second, and is cheerful anyway, because he has a fare and the meter is running and it is nearly the new year.

A film gets that feeling from hindsight and a score. Here you get it in a conversation, from somebody being perfectly reasonable, and there is nothing you can do about it.

New walk: The Last Year of the Century. Colombo, 1999.
posts.instagram:
MILLENNIUM PARTY, 1999 to 2000. Colombo, the last weeks of December.

Ask him about Y2K and he will tell you what people are saying in the back of his three-wheeler. He does not know it comes to nothing. He does not know how long the war has left.

You know both. You cannot tell him. 🛺
posts.twitter:
That banner says MILLENNIUM PARTY 1999 to 2000. Colombo, December.

Ask our guide about Y2K and he'll tell you what his passengers are saying. He doesn't know it comes to nothing.

You do. You can't tell him. That gap is the whole feeling.

posts.title: Touch anything in the picture
posts.hook: The quieter way to ask. Touch a thing in the scene and the guide tells you about that thing.
posts.linkedin:
There are two dots in this frame, and they are the second way to ask a question.

Holding the button and speaking is the one people notice. This is the quiet one. Every scene in every walk carries points you can simply touch, and the guide answers about that thing, in his own voice, without stopping the walk.

This is the covered market in Istanbul in 1616. Touch the domed hall behind the awnings and Yusuf, who carries water for a living, tells you those strongrooms are the market's anchors: one is the old bedesten, where silk and jewellery sit behind thick walls and iron doors, and the other is Sandal, named for the cloth sold in it. Touch the stall at the bottom left and you get the booksellers, who settled beside the bedesten long before his time, and who are still how a stranger finds his way, because men ask for the gate with the books when they do not know the lane.

Stay in this one stop and there are more. Who actually sets the price of bread, and the crier who carries it through the markets. Brokers whose hands are too friendly with one another, holding a seller's goods low and splitting the difference. Why a customer stroking the red atlas cloth is really feeling out his own purse, at two hundred akçe the zira'.

None of that is in the narration. A tap answers about the thing you touched, not about the scene you are already listening to, so the depth is there if you want it and invisible if you do not.

How long a walk takes is therefore up to you rather than to us.
posts.instagram:
See the dots? Touch one.

The domed hall is the bedesten, where silk and jewellery sit behind iron doors. The stall on the left is the booksellers, and men still ask for the gate with the books when they cannot find the lane.

None of that is in the narration. It is there if you are curious. 📚

Istanbul, 1616.

tour_london_1666_waterman.linkedin:
In the first week of September 1666, the safest place in London was the river.

Will Chandler was a licensed waterman at Old Swan Stairs, seven years apprenticed, rowing a pair of oars. That week he carried furniture, plate and frightened families downriver while the City burned behind them, and he watched the price of a boat go up by the hour.

He is dry about it. He is not impressed by gentlemen. And he will take you along five stops of a city in the act of disappearing.

New walk: The Fire and the Waterman. London, 1666.

tour_london_1755_coffee_house.hook: A city running on coffee, news and credit.
tour_london_1755_coffee_house.linkedin:
Georgian London ran on coffee, news, credit and gin, and most of it was transacted in rooms like Hannah Pyke's.

She keeps a coffee house off Fleet Street. Merchants, printers and ships' captains read the papers there and do business she is not supposed to overhear. She overhears it. She is widowed, practical, funny and entirely unshockable, and she knows what everyone in the room is worth.

Five stops through the city that invented the modern news cycle, led by the woman pouring.

New walk: The Coffee House and the New Bridge. London, 1755.

tour_london_1850_flower_seller.hook: Violets bought before six, sold on Ludgate Hill.
tour_london_1850_flower_seller.linkedin:
Nell Baker is thirty-one, widowed, with two children, and she is at Covent Garden before six in the morning to buy violets, wallflowers and watercress.

Then she stands on Ludgate Hill with a basket and sells them, in the spring of 1850, in a London of new railways and old smells.

She is sharp, warm and very funny, and she will walk you from St Paul's down to the river telling you what things cost, who buys them, and how you tell a good bunch from a bad one.

tour_london_1908_conductor.hook: The horse buses are dying and he knows it.
tour_london_1908_conductor.linkedin:
Ernie Marsh has been on the buses six years, three of them behind horses before the motors came.

He is twenty-nine, from Bermondsey, a talker by trade, and he is proud of knowing every fare and every short cut in London. He is also watching his trade change under him: the horse buses are dying, electricity is arriving, and nobody has told him what happens to the men who knew the horses.

Five stops across Edwardian London from the platform of a motor omnibus.

tour_rome_1600_herb_seller.hook: The market and the executions share a square.
tour_rome_1600_herb_seller.linkedin:
Caterina Ruspoli sells herbs in Campo de' Fiori, where the market runs every morning and the executions happen in the same square.

In February of 1600 she watched a friar burned there. She will tell you what the crowd was like. Then she will go back to selling greens, because it is the Jubilee, Rome is full of pilgrims, and a stall does not mind itself.

Blunt, kind, quietly devout and quietly sceptical. Five stops through a city of scaffolding and pilgrims with the new St Peter's rising over the old one.

tour_rome_1750_cicerone.linkedin:
Domenico Fabbri walks English, French and German gentlemen round the antiquities of Rome for a fee. He learned his Latin from a priest and his English from his customers.

He is forty-four, charming, mercenary, and extremely good at knowing what a young Englishman on the Grand Tour wants to be told. Half the city is a building site and half of it is two thousand years old, and he will show you both while relieving you of your money.

The original tour guide, guiding you.

tour_rome_1870_seamstress.hook: The year the Pope lost Rome.
tour_rome_1870_seamstress.linkedin:
In September 1870 the Italian army breached the wall at Porta Pia, and the Papal States ended.

Assunta Belli watched it from a rooftop. She is twenty-nine, a seamstress near the river, and she takes in sewing from households on both sides of that argument, which is why she is careful about what she says out loud.

She has opinions. She voted for nothing, being a woman. She will walk you through five stops of a city changing hands, and she will tell you which of her customers stopped speaking to which.

New walk: The Year Everything Changed. Rome, 1870.

tour_stockholm_1650_porter.hook: A wooden capital grown rich on copper.
tour_stockholm_1650_porter.linkedin:
In 1650 Stockholm was a small wooden capital that had grown rich on copper, iron and a long war, and all of it came across the Skeppsbron quay on somebody's back.

Olof Nilsson's back, for instance. He is thirty-six, up from a farm in Uppland at fifteen, and he carries and stacks copper plates, iron bars, salt and cloth. Strong, dry, watchful. A Lutheran who works on saints' days because the cargo does not keep.

Five stops through Queen Christina's harbour with the man moving it.

tour_stockholm_1755_tavern.hook: A parliament that argues in public, and a tavern that hears it.
tour_stockholm_1755_tavern.linkedin:
Sweden's Age of Liberty had a parliament that argued in public, and the arguing did not stop at the door.

Britta Lindqvist keeps a tavern on Stortorget, the main square, where clerks, sailors and minor gentlemen drink beer, brandy and coffee and settle the affairs of the nation loudly enough to be heard on the stairs. She is forty-one, widowed, shrewd, warm, and unimpressed by all of them.

Five stops through a city where politics was a spectator sport, told from behind the bar.

tour_stockholm_1900_tram.hook: Nine years on the horse trams, and the electric is coming.
tour_stockholm_1900_tram.linkedin:
Gustav Ek has been a conductor on the horse trams for nine years. He is thirty-three, married, three children in two rooms on Södermalm, and he is proud of his line.

He is also quietly worried, because there is electric light on the main streets now and everybody can see what is coming for the horses.

Five stops through Stockholm at the turn of the century, with a man who can feel his own job ending and is too polite to say so directly.

tour_colombo_1700_cinnamon.hook: The bark that paid for a colony.
tour_colombo_1700_cinnamon.linkedin:
In 1700 the Dutch East India Company held the coast of Ceylon, and what paid for it was cinnamon.

Kumari peels it. She is thirty-four, of the Salagama community, working the Company's quota with her family: cutting the shoots, scraping the bark, rolling the quills to dry. It takes years to learn to do it without tearing, and she is quietly proud of that.

She is also working to a number set by men she will never meet, in a city built to move her work to Amsterdam.

tour_colombo_1905_rickshaw.hook: Ten hours a day barefoot on hot tar.
tour_colombo_1905_rickshaw.linkedin:
Sena is twenty-seven and pulls a rickshaw for hire in Colombo's Fort and Pettah: ten hours a day, barefoot on hot tar, renting the vehicle by the day from a man who owns thirty of them.

He came down from a village up the coast at seventeen. Behind him the harbour sits behind its new breakwater, one of the great coaling stations of the empire, and everything in the city is arriving or leaving.

Five stops through British Colombo at street level, from the one person who sees all of it and is paid by the trip.

tour_istanbul_1616_water_carrier.hook: A city on seven hills, and the man who carries the water up them.
tour_istanbul_1616_water_carrier.linkedin:
Istanbul in 1616 drinks from aqueducts a thousand years old, and none of that water reaches the top of a hill on its own.

Yusuf is thirty-one, a saka. He fills a leather skin at a fountain and carries it up to the houses, shops and workrooms that have none of their own, paid by the trip. He came from a village in Anatolia as a boy and lodges above a bakehouse near the Süleymaniye. He knows which spouts run sweet, which run dry in August, which gatekeeper will let him cut through a courtyard, and which houses make him come back twice for his money.

He carries water to Greeks, Armenians, Jews and Franks as readily as to anyone, because giving water is a good deed as well as a trade, and a saka is never quite only a tradesman.

The Sultan's new mosque on the Hippodrome is finished this year and the scaffolding is coming down. Five stops, reading the city by its water: the race ground, the covered market, the third hill, the landing stages, and Galata on the far shore where the rules are not quite the same.

New walk: The City's Thirst. Istanbul, 1616.

tour_istanbul_1660_midwife.hook: In July the city burned for forty-nine hours. She kept walking to births.
tour_istanbul_1660_midwife.linkedin:
In July 1660 a fire ran for forty-nine hours through the timber quarters between the Golden Horn and the market, and took a great part of Istanbul with it.

Emine is forty-four, an ebe, a midwife. She is called out at any hour to her own quarter and the ones next to it, and she is let into all of them: Muslim, Greek, Armenian and Jewish houses alike, because a birth does not wait for anyone to agree about religion. She is paid in coin, or cloth, or a share of the sweets. Her mother-in-law taught her the work and twenty years taught her the rest.

This year she walks to births through streets that are not there any more.

She is plain spoken, unshockable, kind without being soft, and very tired. She does not know what the Valide Sultan will finish building, or how long the war will run. Five stops: the burnt ground, a quarter the fire missed, the women's bath where she learns more than at any threshold, the great mosque starting again out of the ash, and the crossing to the other shore at evening.

New walk: The Year the City Burned. Istanbul, 1660.

tour_colombo_1999_three_wheeler.hook: The last year of the century, from the driver's seat of a hired three-wheeler.
tour_colombo_1999_three_wheeler.linkedin:
Colombo, December 1999. There is a presidential election, a bomb at a rally, and a rumour going round that the computers will stop at midnight on the thirty-first.

Ranjith is thirty-four and drives a red Bajaj three-wheeler he rents by the day from a man in Dematagoda, so he pays the owner and the petrol before he earns a rupee for the house. He was a lorry helper and then a bus conductor before this. His wife works in a cloth shop in Pettah and the two children are at school in Maradana. He knows every junction, every shortcut, every checkpoint and which of the soldiers on them are decent, and he carries Sinhala, Tamil, Muslim and Burgher passengers without pretending the city is one people.

The Fort is a sealed high-security zone three years after the Central Bank bomb, so he noses in to the barrier and lets the fare walk the last part. The World Trade Centre towers are two years old and still look, he says, as though Fort has put on a foreign suit and has not broken it in yet.

Six stops at street level, with the meter running.
